tagline.text: Spanish-era coral-stone coastal watchtowers and the sunset spot of Luna's Baluarte

location.label: Location
location.text: La Union coast (Luna, Balaoan, San Juan, San Fernando and Bacnotan)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~1,500 (La Union day trip, excluding round-trip transport from Manila)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Clark International Airport (CRK) or Laoag International Airport (LAO)

children.text: The La Union coast still holds round coral-stone watchtowers that the Spanish built to watch for Moro and Chinese pirates. They were declared National Cultural Treasures in 2014, and Luna's Baluarte is the best known and a well-loved sunset spot.

Along the west coast of La Union, facing the South China Sea (the West Philippine Sea), a few round coral-stone watchtowers remain. Locals call them baluarte or bantayan. They were built during the Spanish colonial period as lookouts so that coastal villages could spot Moro and Chinese pirates before a raid. They are cylindrical towers roughly
tall, said to be built of coral blocks and adobe (tuff) bricks bound with a mortar of lime and egg white.

The towers that appear in Wikipedia and National Museum–related sources are the Baluarte in Luna, the Almeida watchtower in Balaoan, the Ili Sur watchtower in San Juan, the Carlatan watchtower in San Fernando City, and the Bacnotan watchtower. Of these, the Baluarte is the easiest to reach and the most photographed. Records say the National Museum declared these La Union towers National Cultural Treasures in November 2014. Several of them, however, stand on private property and cannot be entered.

The appeal here is not flashy sights but coastal scenery and history: an old round tower standing on a pebble beach, a structure half rebuilt with new bricks, and the sea turning red at sunset. It fits easily into a day trip heading north from the surf towns of San Juan and San Fernando. Sources disagree on the construction date, so this guide states only that these are watchtowers from the Spanish colonial period and gives no exact year. The restoration reportedly used materials similar to the original ones, so look for the line where old and new bricks meet to read the tower's long history.
Luna is about
267 km
from Manila and about
north of San Fernando. A same-day round trip from Manila is therefore long, and the most realistic plan is to stay in San Juan or San Fernando and visit for half a day.

This round watchtower stands on the pebble beach of Barangay Victoria in Luna and is the most famous of the La Union towers. Coastal erosion split it in two, and after restoration one side is new brick and the other is original. It is described as free to visit. A circular wooden boardwalk surrounds the tower, and the spot is known for wedding photos and sunset watching. The light coming off the sea as the sun lowers makes for good photos. Along the nearby shore you may see colorful pebbles sorted and sold as decorations, but pebble collection is regulated, so do not take any home.
In October 2015, Typhoon Lando (Koppu) brought down the half that had been leaning toward the sea. It was then rebuilt for about
using materials similar to the original ones, and a June 2017 report describes the work as completed.

This tower stands on the coast of Barangay Almeida in Balaoan, and Wikipedia lists it as marked by the National Museum. It is said to have formed a coastal defense line together with the towers of Luna, Bacnotan and San Juan.

It stands on the coast of Barangay Ili Sur in San Juan and is described as having served as a base for US and Filipino guerrilla forces (USAFIP-NL) during World War II. Visitors report that only part of the original remains and the rest is a reconstruction, so check its condition before you go.

This tower is inside a beachfront resort property in Carlatan, San Fernando City. Because it is private land, access may be restricted. A blog record says the interior was once altered and used as a guest room.
It is known to stand on high ground in Bacnotan inside a fenced private lot, so it cannot be seen up close. It is the hardest of the five La Union watchtowers to reach.
Head north from San Juan or San Fernando. Jeepneys to Luna run along the national highway. From San Juan, look for one bound for Luna, and from San Fernando there are direct jeepneys.
In Luna town, stop by St. Catherine of Alexandria Church (Namacpacan Church) for a short visit. It is known as a National Cultural Treasure.
From the church, walk or take a tricycle west toward the beach to the Baluarte in Barangay Victoria. The ground is pebbles, so wear comfortable shoes.
Walk around the tower, compare the restored bricks with the old ones, and wait for sunset on the circular boardwalk.
After dark, return to town by jeepney or tricycle, have dinner, and head back to your lodging. Check your ride back before it gets dark.
Luna is a small town and transport thins out late in the evening. Confirm the last jeepney and shared-ride times locally.
Start from San Fernando. The Carlatan watchtower is on private land, so view it from the road or outside, or ask resort staff for permission first.
Move on to the Ili Sur coast in San Juan to see the tower. It is a surf town, so a beachside cafe makes a good rest stop.
Have lunch as you pass through Bacnotan. The Bacnotan tower is inside a fence, so you may only see it from a distance.
Visit the Luna Baluarte and spend the most time here. Leave plenty of time for photos.
Continue north to Balaoan to see the Almeida coastal tower. The way is down a seaside lane, so check the location on a map app and ask locals for directions.
Catch a southbound or northbound bus from the Balaoan terminal.
Seeing all five in a day means a lot of travel and some you cannot enter. We recommend centering the day on the Luna Baluarte and choosing two or three others.

Long-distance buses from Manila (around Cubao and Santa Cruz) toward Ilocos, Vigan and Laoag pass through La Union. Companies such as Partas, Dominion, Fariñas and Philippine Rabbit are known to run these routes.
Tell the conductor the nearest of San Fernando La Union, San Juan or Bacnotan. If the bus goes as far as Luna or Balaoan, give the conductor that town's name.
Luna is about
267 km
from Manila. Travel time and fares vary a great deal by time of day and traffic, so check current information before you leave.
A same-day round trip from Manila is hard. Staying one night in San Fernando or San Juan is easier.
The nearest air route is to Laoag (LAO), but it is far from the southern La Union coast.
You can also take a bus or van from Clark International Airport (CRK) toward San Fernando. Connections change by season, so check them.
Jeepneys to Luna run along the national highway from San Fernando and San Juan.
Because the towers are down seaside lanes, hiring a tricycle for a few hours is convenient. Agree on stops and the fare before boarding, as it varies with distance and season, and haggle if needed.
With a rental car or your own car, it is easy to move between the towers along a single national highway.
La Union has a dry season from November to May, with many clear days and good sunsets. The light on the tower in the late afternoon is especially good for photos.
From June to early November it is rainy and typhoons often pass along the coast. High waves make the pebble beach dangerous, and the Baluarte was in fact badly damaged by a typhoon in 2015.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Best for sunsets and photos. The coast is crowded around New Year and on weekends.
The midday sun is strong, so visit in the morning or late afternoon.
Rough waves can make travel difficult, so check the weather forecast.

Luna is a small town with few places to stay. Most travelers stay in the surf towns of San Juan or San Fernando and make a day trip to Luna. San Juan beach has many guesthouses and hostels, so it is easy to choose one that fits your plans.

In Luna town you can try Ilocano snacks and regional dishes. One travel account mentions tasting bibingka near the church. Opening hours vary and some places close early in the evening, so check ahead for dinner after sunset.

In the surf season, lodging near San Juan beach fills up quickly. Book ahead for weekends and holidays, and choose where to stay with the thinning evening transport back from Luna in mind. You can pick up simple snacks at roadside shops along the highway, but there are almost no shops near the towers, so bring water and snacks.
Go in the late afternoon to the Baluarte to capture both the sunset and the tower. Check your ride back before it gets dark.
The beach is pebbles, so sturdy-soled sneakers are better than sandals.
Do not enter towers on private property past a fence or gate without permission. If you want to take photos, ask the staff first.
Pebble collection on the beach is regulated and contributes to erosion, so do not take any.
The roads to the Almeida tower in Balaoan and the Darigayos shore near Luna can be narrow and poorly signed, so save an offline map.
Combining Namacpacan Church in Luna and Darigayos Cove makes for a full day.
Right after rain the waves get higher, so do not go down to the beach near the tower.
There is almost no shade near the towers. Bring a hat, sunscreen and water, and avoid visiting at midday.

Each tower is in a different state of preservation, so rather than trying to see them all, the Luna Baluarte plus one or two others gives the best experience. Ask the La Union tourism office or your local lodging about access and directions.
Some towers are on private land or behind fences and cannot be entered, and the beach is dangerous in typhoon season. Check access and the weather before you leave.
Do not enter the Carlatan and Bacnotan towers without permission, as they are on private property.
Below the Luna Baluarte is a pebble beach eroded by waves and not suited to swimming. The nearby Nalvo shore also has strong currents and drops off steeply.
Do not climb or write graffiti on the tower walls. They are National Cultural Treasures.
The condition of restoration and damage varies among towers, and what you see may differ from photos, so keep your expectations modest.
When a typhoon is approaching, avoid the coast and follow local government announcements.
This beach town is famous for surfing, has the Ili Sur watchtower, and is a good base for catching jeepneys to Luna. Jeepneys to Luna are boarded on the national highway.

blocks.title: San Fernando La Union History and Coast

children.text: The provincial capital has the Carlatan watchtower and many places to stay and eat, making it a good starting point for the trip.
If you have another day after the watchtowers, you can add a waterfall trek in the San Gabriel area.
Farther north is Vigan, with its Spanish colonial city heritage, a good way to continue a history-themed trip.
